Experiments and Discussions To validate our implementation, we benchmark coverforest’s three methods: CV+, J+ab, and split conformal on conformal classfication and regression tasks. We compare our imple- mentations against the most recent packages for conformal predictions, namely the crepes and MAPIE packages. 5.1 Classification experiment We evaluate the predictions and run times of CoverForestClassifier on five classification datasets, namely Mice [32], WineQuality [33], Bean [34], MNIST, and Helena [35] datasets. See Table 3 for the datasets’ characteristics. We aim to evaluate the methods’ abilities to achieve the desired level of coverage even with a few training points. To this end, we randomly select 20% of the dataset as the test set (except the MNIST dataset whose test set has already been prepared), and 200 rows of the remaining data as the training set. For the split conformal method, we reserve 100 rows of the training set as the calibration set. We then fit the models on the training set with the target miscoverage level α ∈ {0.05,0.1,0.2}. We repeat the experiment 50 times for each method and compare the empirical coverage (the proportion of prediction sets that contain the true class), and average set size. For CV+, we split the training data into 10 folds, and each random forest has 30 trees. For J+ab and split conformal, the random forest has 100 trees. Conclusion In this work, we introduce coverforest, a lightweight package that bridges the gap be- tween scikit-learn’s optimized random forest implementation and modern conformal pre- diction techniques. By leveraging both cross-validation+ and Jackknife+-after-bootstrap approaches, coverforest enables uncertainty quantification through distribution-free pre- diction intervals and prediction sets. Our empirical evaluation demonstrates that coverforest not only achieves the desired coverage guarantees but is also faster than existing implementation of conformal predic- tions with random forests. Given random forest’s established effectiveness on tabular data, coverforest provides a practical solution for deployment of conformal prediction in real- 17 world applications. Future work could explore extensions to other ensemble methods and conformal prediction techniques while maintaining the package’s emphasis on simplicity and efficiency. Finally,weacknowledgeacurrentlimitationofourpackageregardingcomputationalscal- ability. The implementation is highly optimized for multi-core CPU execution via Cython, but it does not currently support GPU acceleration or distributed computing. A significant avenue for future work is to extend the framework to leverage GPU-native libraries, such as cuML [42], or distributed platforms like Dask [43] and Ray [44] While this would require a substantialchangetothecodebase,itwouldgreatlyenhancetheapplicabilityofourmethods to large-scale datasets that exceed the capabilities of a single machine. JSON: Name: coverforest_pipeline Title: Efficient conformal prediction with random forests: optimized cross-conformal and jackknife+-after-bootstrap procedures for calibrated prediction sets and intervals Short Hypothesis: Applying parallelized out-of-bag aggregation and Cython-optimized cross-conformity computations to scikit-learn random forests will reduce end-to-end CV+ and J+ab prediction time by at least 2x relative to existing Python implementations while maintaining empirical coverage ≥ nominal (1−α) across benchmark classification and regression datasets. Related Work: Conformal prediction provides distribution-free calibrated prediction intervals and sets via split conformal, cross-validation+ (CV+), and jackknife+-after-bootstrap (J+ab) procedures; adaptive scores for classification include APS and RAPS. Prior software packages implement subsets of these methods but trade off data efficiency, coverage guarantees, or runtime: split/inductive conformal is fast but data-inefficient; CV+ and J+ab are more data-efficient but incur high O(n_train * n_test * C) pairwise costs and limited optimized implementations. Bootstrapped J+ab attains finite-sample guarantees only with randomized bootstrap counts; many prior proposals use OOB heuristics without finite-sample guarantees or require extensive serial Python loops, causing high memory/time usage. Existing libraries (nonconformist, crepes, MAPIE) provide partial functionality (APS/RAPS, CV+, J+ab) but either lack J+ab for classification, lack RAPS auto-search, or do not exploit low-level optimizations and parallel OOB aggregation. Abstract: This research pipeline targets scalable, distribution-free uncertainty quantification for random-forest predictors by optimizing conformal prediction procedures that rely on out-of-fold/out-of-bag computations. We propose to integrate parallel tree fitting and query paths of standard random-forest implementations with Cython-accelerated cross-conformity-score calculations to implement split conformal, CV+, and Jackknife+-after-Bootstrap (J+ab) for regression and APS/RAPS-based set predictions for classification. The primary contribution is a reproducible experimental evaluation comparing runtime, memory, empirical coverage, and prediction-set/interval size against existing Python conformal packages and ablations that isolate the impact of OOB aggregation, randomized bootstrap counts, and RAPS regularization. Expected outcomes are (1) measurable runtime and memory improvements for CV+ and J+ab without coverage loss, (2) quantification of trade-offs between data efficiency and set size for APS vs. RAPS, and (3) operational guidance for applying these optimized conformal workflows on tabular datasets. The pipeline focuses on verifiable, repeatable experiments and clear failure modes for scalability and coverage. Experiments: Datasets: classification: Mice (8 features, multi-class), WineQuality (11), Bean (16), MNIST (784), Helena (27, 100 classes); regression: Housing, Concrete, Bike, Crime. Data splits: for each dataset repeat 50 trials with random seed: hold out 20% test set; from remaining data sample n_train=200 for main comparisons; for scaling experiments use full available training sets. Methods to compare: (A) optimized implementation (parallel OOB aggregation + Cython cross-conformity) implementing split, CV+ (K=10), J+ab (B ̃=n_estimators; resample randomized per Binomial(B ̃,(1−m/n)) enabled); APS and RAPS scores with k_init and lambda_init auto-search; (B) MAPIE implementation; (C) crepes implementation (OOB and split where available); (D) baseline scikit-learn random forest + naive Python conformal loops. Hyperparameters: n_estimators: CV+ uses 100 forests × 10 trees each (equivalently 1000 total trees) or alternative settings {30,100,400,900} for sensitivity; for J+ab and split use n_estimators ∈ {100,400,900}; α ∈ {0.05,0.10,0.20}. Evaluation metrics: empirical coverage (proportion of test points with true label/value inside set/interval), average prediction set size (classification) or average interval length (regression), standard error of coverage, training time, prediction time, peak memory usage. Experiments and ablations: 1) Main comparison: measure metrics for methods A–D across datasets and α values. 2) Ablation on optimizations: disable Cython cross-conformity, disable parallel OOB aggregation, vary num_threads ∈ {1,4,8,16} to quantify speedups. 3) J+ab bootstrap randomness: compare fixed-B vs randomized-B on empirical coverage and variance. 4) APS vs RAPS: compare average set sizes and coverages and perform grid search ablation on k_init, lambda_init. 5) Scaling study: increase n_train ∈ {200,1000,full} and n_test ∈ {200,1000,5000} to measure time and memory growth, report O(n_train * n_test * C) behavior. Statistical reporting: report mean ± SE over 50 trials; perform one-sided t-tests for coverage ≥ 1−α and pairwise t-tests for set sizes/interval lengths, with significance levels 0.05, 0.01, 0.001. Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Computational complexity: CV+ and J+ab with APS/RAPS incur O(n_train * n_test * C) time and memory for full cross-conformity comparisons; large n_train, n_test, or C may exceed single-machine memory and negate speed gains. 2) Non-exchangeability: coverage guarantees assume exchangeable data; real-world distribution shifts or temporal dependence invalidate finite-sample guarantees. 3) OOB bias and bootstrap randomness: OOB aggregation and randomized bootstrap counts can introduce additional variance or bias in small samples, potentially lowering empirical coverage. 4) Class imbalance and many classes: APS/RAPS behavior can produce large sets or empty sets for extreme imbalance or high C; RAPS regularization may over- or under-penalize depending on hyperparameters. 5) Reliance on scikit-learn internals: changes in scikit-learn random-forest internals, platform-specific parallel scheduling, or thread contention may affect reproducibility and performance. 6) Lack of GPU/distributed support: current optimizations target multi-core CPU; scaling to very large datasets requires substantial re-engineering for GPU or distributed frameworks. 7) Evaluation bias: using primarily tabular benchmarks may not generalize to structured data (text, images) or to models other than random forests.
